t-inside.overview: Every frontier LLM today is a **decoder-only transformer**, and this part of the map opens one up, using DeepSeek-V3's public `config.json` as the worked example because closed models don't publish their shapes. Text is chopped into [tokens](#c/tokenizer) (vocabulary 129,280), each token becomes a 7,168-wide [embedding](#c/embedding) vector, and that vector rises through a [stack of 61 layers](#c/layer-stack). Each layer does two things: [attention](#c/attention), where tokens read from one another through 128 query/key/value heads, and a [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) that works on each token alone (here a Mixture of Experts). Only after the last layer does the [output head](#c/output-head) turn the vector into next-token probabilities. Around this core sits a family of efficiency tricks (GQA, MLA, sparse attention, FlashAttention, PagedAttention, KV quantization, prefix caching, RoPE scaling) that the chat sorted into two kinds: ones baked in at training time and ones that make an already-frozen model cheaper to serve.

transformer.overview: A **decoder-only transformer** is the architecture behind every current frontier LLM. It reads a sequence of [tokens](#c/tokenizer), turns each into a vector, and passes all the vectors up through a stack of identical-shaped but independently trained [layers](#c/layer-stack). Each layer mixes information across tokens with [attention](#c/attention), then processes each token on its own with a [feed-forward network](#c/ffn). A final [output head](#c/output-head) turns the top vector into a probability for every possible next token. The model then samples one token, appends it, and repeats. DeepSeek-V3, whose config is public, is a concrete instance: 61 layers, a 7,168-wide residual stream, 128 attention heads per layer, 256 routed experts per MoE layer, a 129,280-token vocabulary and a 160K context. Closed models (Claude, GPT, Gemini) are built on the same skeleton, but their layer counts and widths are undisclosed.
transformer.article:
A **decoder-only transformer** is a neural network that predicts the next [token](#c/tokenizer) in a sequence from all the tokens before it. It descends from the 2017 "Attention Is All You Need" Transformer, which had an encoder and a decoder with 6 layers each. GPT-style language models kept only the decoder half and scaled it up enormously. Every current frontier LLM is built this way. The specific numbers below come from DeepSeek-V3, whose `config.json` is public. Closed models share the same structure, but their exact shapes aren't published.

## The pipeline, end to end

1. **Tokenize.** Text is split into tokens from a fixed vocabulary (129,280 entries for DeepSeek-V3).
2. **Embed.** Each token id picks out one row of an [embedding](#c/embedding) table, giving a vector of `hidden_size` = 7,168 numbers.
3. **Refine through the layer stack.** The vectors pass up through [61 layers](#c/layer-stack). Each layer reads the running vector and *adds* an adjustment to it, which is why the running vector is called the [residual stream](#c/residual).
4. **Unembed.** The final vector for the last position is projected by the [output head](#c/output-head) into 129,280 scores (logits), and a softmax turns those into a probability distribution over the next token.
5. **Sample and repeat.** One token is chosen, appended to the input, and the [decoding loop](#c/decoding) runs again.

## Inside one layer

Every layer (a "transformer block") has the same two sub-parts, each wrapped in normalization and a residual connection:

| Sub-part | What it does | DeepSeek-V3 |
|---|---|---|
| [Attention](#c/attention) | The only place tokens exchange information. Each token's query is matched against earlier tokens' keys, and their values are pulled in. | 128 [heads](#c/heads), compressed with [MLA](#c/mla) |
| [Feed-forward network](#c/ffn) | Processes each token on its own; much stored knowledge lives here | First 3 layers dense (width 18,432); remaining 58 are [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe): 8 of 256 routed [experts](#c/experts) plus 1 [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) |

Each layer has its *own* private weights: layer 1's heads and layer 40's heads share nothing. Depth adds genuinely new transformations rather than repeating one, and each layer also keeps its own slice of the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache).

## Why "decoder-only"

"Decoder" here means the attention is **causal**: a token can only look at tokens before it, never after. That makes the model a natural next-token predictor and lets past computations be cached. When the model generates, the keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so they are stored once in the KV-cache rather than recomputed at every step. That cache, not the arithmetic, turns out to be the main pressure on serving cost.

## Size and cost

A dense transformer runs every parameter for every token. MoE breaks that link: DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B parameters but activates only about 37B per token. Total parameters buy capacity; active parameters set the per-token cost. On the attention side, techniques like [GQA](#c/gqa) and MLA shrink the cache. The whole thing runs inside a [serving system](#c/serving) that batches many users' requests together and uses low-precision numbers (DeepSeek ships its weights natively in FP8).

## Trade-offs and limits

Attention compares every token with every earlier token, so its cost grows quadratically with context length, and the KV-cache grows linearly. Most architecture work since 2017 has attacked those two costs, through sparse and [linear/hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn), cache compression, or dropping attention altogether in [state-space models](#c/ssm). Autoregressive decoding is also strictly sequential, one token per step, which is what [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding) and [diffusion LMs](#c/diffusion-lm) try to get around.

## From the chat

- The chat said plainly that this "standard decoder-only transformer … every current frontier LLM is built on" is solid architecture, not provider-specific guesswork. What is *not* public is how many layers, heads or how much width Claude, GPT-4-class models or Gemini use.
- It corrected the idea that layers each predict a token and blend their guesses. There is exactly one prediction, made from the final layer's output.
- It pulled DeepSeek-V3's real `config.json`: 61 layers (3 dense + 58 MoE), hidden 7,168, 256 experts (8 routed + 1 shared active), 128 heads, MLA with a 512-dim latent, vocabulary 129,280, 160K context via YaRN.
- It stressed that DeepSeek's weights and inference code are open, and some training infrastructure too, but not the training data or a turnkey from-scratch training pipeline.

tokenizer.overview: A **tokenizer** is the step before the network ever sees text: it chops the input into **tokens** drawn from a fixed vocabulary, usually subword pieces learned by a byte-pair-encoding-style algorithm, so common words are one token and rare words split into several. Each token becomes an integer id, and that id is all the model receives. DeepSeek-V3's vocabulary has **129,280** entries. That number sets the number of rows in the [embedding](#c/embedding) table and the number of scores the [output head](#c/output-head) produces at every step. Tokens are also the unit of cost: API prices, [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) size and generation speed are all counted in them. Tokenization has side effects. Models famously miscount letters in a word because they see chunks, not characters, which is why tokenizer-free designs like the [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/blt) exist.
tokenizer.article:
A **tokenizer** converts raw text into a sequence of integer ids, called **tokens**, that a [transformer](#c/transformer) can process, and converts ids back into text on the way out. It is not itself a neural network layer. It is a fixed lookup procedure built before training, and every downstream part of the model is shaped around it.

## How it works

Most LLM tokenizers use a **subword** scheme such as byte-pair encoding (BPE). Starting from individual bytes or characters, the training procedure repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new vocabulary entry until the vocabulary reaches a target size. The result:

- very common words ("the", " and") become a single token, often including the leading space;
- less common words split into a few familiar pieces;
- anything at all can still be represented, falling back to bytes if needed.

At inference time the tokenizer applies the learned merges to the input and emits a list of ids. Each id is then used to look up a row of the [embedding](#c/embedding) table.

## Why vocabulary size matters

DeepSeek-V3's config lists `vocab_size: 129280`. That single number shows up at both ends of the model:

| Where | Shape in DeepSeek-V3 |
|---|---|
| Embedding table (id → vector) | 129,280 × 7,168 |
| [Output head](#c/output-head) (vector → score per token) | 7,168 × 129,280 |

Each matrix is about 0.93 billion parameters. A larger vocabulary packs more text into each token, so sequences get shorter and attention gets cheaper, but it makes these two matrices bigger and spreads training signal across more rare entries. A smaller vocabulary does the opposite. The choice is a design trade-off rather than something with one right answer.

## Tokens as the unit of everything

Because the model only ever sees tokens, almost every cost in the system is counted in them:

- **Price.** API providers bill per input and output token.
- **Memory.** The [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) stores keys and values per token, per layer.
- **Speed.** Autoregressive [decoding](#c/decoding) produces one token per step.
- **Context length.** Limits like DeepSeek-V3's 163,840 positions are counted in tokens, not characters or words.

So a tokenizer that compresses text more efficiently in some language or domain makes the model cheaper and effectively longer-context for that content.

## Trade-offs and limits

Tokenization is lossy with respect to *spelling*. The model sees "strawberry" as one or a few opaque chunks, not as letters, so questions about individual characters (counting letters, reversing strings) are unexpectedly hard. The chat called this "a tokenization artifact, not a reasoning failure." A tokenizer also freezes early decisions: its merges are learned from a particular data mix, and text that mix under-represented, such as some languages or code styles, splits into many more tokens.

## Alternatives

The most developed alternative drops the tokenizer entirely. Meta's [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/blt) reads raw bytes and groups them dynamically into patches, spending more compute where the text is harder to predict. The chat reported BLT matching tokenizer-based models such as Llama 3 at the tested scales (1B–8B parameters), and byte-level models scoring near-perfectly on spelling tasks. The mainstream transformer stack, though, still starts with a conventional tokenizer.

## From the chat

- DeepSeek-V3's real config gives `vocab_size: 129280`, which sets the size of both the embedding table and the output projection.
- The chat named the tokenizer as one of the "givens" that alternative architectures attack: "a flawed tokenizer distorts input before the model even begins reasoning."
- Letter-counting failures were explained as a tokenization artifact, and byte-level models do well on spelling for exactly that reason.
- BLT was described as the most developed tokenizer-free design, with parity demonstrated at 1B–8B scale rather than at the frontier.

embedding.overview: The **embedding** is the model's first real layer: a big lookup table with one row per vocabulary entry. When a [token](#c/tokenizer) id comes in, its row is copied out as a vector, and that vector is what flows through the rest of the network. In DeepSeek-V3 the table is 129,280 rows × **7,168** columns (about 0.93B parameters), so every token starts life as 7,168 numbers. That width, `hidden_size`, is *the* central dimension of the model: [attention](#c/attention) reads and writes vectors that wide, the [residual stream](#c/residual) is that wide, and the [output head](#c/output-head) projects from that width back to the vocabulary. The embedding carries no position information and no context. "bank" gets the same starting vector whether it's a river or a lender. The layers above add context, and [positional encoding](#c/position) supplies order.
embedding.article:
An **embedding** maps each discrete [token](#c/tokenizer) id to a dense vector of real numbers that the network can compute with. In a [transformer](#c/transformer) it is the entry point: a learned table, indexed by token id, whose rows become the initial state of the [residual stream](#c/residual).

## How it works

The embedding is a matrix of shape `vocab_size × hidden_size`. Looking up a token means taking its row, with no arithmetic beyond the copy. For DeepSeek-V3:

- `vocab_size` = 129,280
- `hidden_size` = 7,168
- table size = 129,280 × 7,168 ≈ 927 million parameters

So a 10-token prompt becomes a 10 × 7,168 array of numbers before the first [layer](#c/layer-stack) runs. Training adjusts these rows like any other weights, and tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors.

## Hidden size: the model's width

The chat spent time on what `hidden_size: 7168` means concretely. It is the length of the vector representing each token *everywhere* in the model:

- the embedding table outputs vectors of this size;
- every layer's [attention](#c/attention) and [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) read and write vectors of this size;
- the final [output head](#c/output-head) projects from this size to the vocabulary.

Width is one of the three big shape knobs, alongside depth (number of layers) and, in MoE models, expert count. A wider vector lets each token carry more information, but most weight matrices scale with it, so cost does too. The chat noted that as models grew, width has often scaled faster than depth.

The same number is easy to confuse with internal widths. DeepSeek-V3's dense FFN expands to 18,432 inside a layer, and each routed [expert](#c/experts) works in only 2,048. Those are temporary scratch spaces *inside* a sub-block. The residual stream between blocks is always 7,168 wide.

## What the embedding does not contain

- **Context.** "bank" starts with one vector regardless of its sentence. Context comes from attention in later layers.
- **Position.** The lookup is identical at position 1 and position 5,000. Order has to be injected separately; modern models do it with [RoPE](#c/rope), which rotates query and key vectors inside attention rather than adding anything to the embedding.

## Input and output embeddings

The output head is also a vocabulary-by-width matrix, and some models *tie* it to the input embedding (one matrix used both ways) to save parameters. DeepSeek-V3's published weights list input and output embeddings separately, alongside the 61 hidden layers. Tying mostly matters for small models, where these two matrices are a large share of total parameters. At 671B total, the ~0.93B embedding is a rounding error.

## From the chat

- The chat corrected a typo in the question: the hidden size is **7,168**, not 716.
- It defined hidden size as "the width of the residual stream," the length of the vector representing each token as it flows up through the layers, and the central dimension of the whole model.
- It explained the flow as "a token starts as an embedding vector … that vector passes up through the stack, and each layer transforms it," with a prediction made only at the very top.
- It contrasted the 7,168 hidden width with the 2,048 per-expert intermediate width, which is *smaller* than hidden on purpose, unlike a dense FFN.

layer-stack.overview: The **layer stack** is the depth of the transformer: a sequence of blocks, each running [attention](#c/attention) then a [feed-forward network](#c/ffn), that repeatedly refines one vector per token. DeepSeek-V3 has **61** (`num_hidden_layers`): the first 3 have dense FFNs (`first_k_dense_replace: 3`) and the other 58 use Mixture of Experts. Layers run **in sequence, not in parallel**, and each has its own independently learned weights, so layer 3 and layer 40 share nothing, not even their attention heads. Each layer adds an adjustment to the [residual stream](#c/residual) rather than replacing it. Only the last layer's output reaches the [output head](#c/output-head) and becomes a prediction. Typical depths: the 2017 Transformer used 6+6, GPT-2/BERT-era models 12–48, modern ~8B models around 30, and the largest open models 60–100+ (GLM-5 has 80).
layer-stack.article:
The **layer stack** is the sequence of transformer blocks between the [embedding](#c/embedding) and the [output head](#c/output-head). Its depth is one of a model's main shape parameters. It is also the part of the architecture most often misunderstood, because it is tempting to picture many layers each guessing the answer and voting.

## How it works

Each layer takes the current vector for every token (7,168 numbers wide in DeepSeek-V3) and returns an updated vector of the same size. Inside, it runs two sub-blocks in order:

1. **[Attention](#c/attention).** Tokens look at earlier tokens and pull in information. This is the *only* place context moves between positions.
2. **[Feed-forward network](#c/ffn).** Each token is processed on its own. In MoE layers this is where the [router](#c/router) picks [experts](#c/experts).

Both are wrapped in normalization and a residual connection, so each layer *adds* its output to the running vector: the [residual stream](#c/residual). The stack is an assembly line working on one piece. Early layers tend to capture local, surface patterns; later layers more abstract and long-range structure.

## Layers do not each predict a token

This was the main correction in the chat. Layers are **sequential**, and **only the last one connects to a prediction**. Intermediate layers produce *representations*, not guesses. Researchers can peek early by applying the output projection to a middle layer (the "logit lens" or "early exit"), and sometimes read off a rough premature guess, but that is a diagnostic or optimization trick, not how the model normally runs.

## Every layer is its own

In the standard design every layer has completely separate weights: its own Q, K and V projections for every [head](#c/heads), and its own FFN or set of experts. That is why depth adds capability instead of just repetition. It also means that:

- the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) is kept **per layer**, so 61 layers means 61 layers' worth of cached keys and values;
- in an MoE model, routing happens **per layer**, so a token gets a separate expert choice at each of the 58 MoE layers.

## DeepSeek-V3's stack

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `num_hidden_layers` | 61 |
| `first_k_dense_replace` | 3 (layers 1–3 use a dense FFN of width 18,432) |
| MoE layers | 58 (256 routed experts, 8 active, + 1 shared) |
| Heads per layer | 128 |

## How deep is typical?

The chat gave these ranges: the original 2017 Transformer used 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers; GPT-2/BERT-era models 12–48; 7–8B models around 30; the biggest open dense and MoE models 60–100+. GLM-5, for example, has 80. Bigger models get both wider and deeper, but pure depth has diminishing returns: doubling layers doesn't double capability, and training gets harder. Architects balance depth, width and expert count by experiment. Closed frontier models' layer counts are not disclosed.

## Variations on the stack

- **[Cross-layer parameter sharing](#c/layer-sharing).** Reuse one layer's weights across the stack (ALBERT). Saves memory, not compute.
- **[Cross-layer KV-cache sharing](#c/kv-sharing).** Adjacent layers share one K/V cache.
- **[Layer pruning](#c/layer-pruning).** Many middle and late layers turn out to do little and can be removed with modest loss.
- **[Hybrids](#c/hybrids).** Swap most attention layers for state-space or linear layers and keep a few full-attention ones.
- **[Recurrent depth](#c/latent-reasoning).** Loop a block a variable number of times instead of stacking distinct ones.

## From the chat

- "Layers do not each predict a token": they are a sequential refinement pipeline feeding a single prediction at the top, not parallel voters.
- Every layer has its own separate query, key and value heads; nothing is shared in the standard design.
- The real DeepSeek-V3 figure is 61 layers, 3 dense + 58 MoE, which corrected earlier secondhand numbers.
- Research finds many middle and late layers in big models are near-identity and prunable. Forced similarity (sharing) trades capability for memory; emergent similarity (redundancy) is waste.
- Layer counts for Claude, GPT-4-class models and Gemini were declined as undisclosed rather than guessed.

attention.overview: **Attention** is the one place in a transformer where tokens exchange information. For each token, every [head](#c/heads) projects a **query** ("what am I looking for"), and every earlier token offers a **key** ("what I advertise") and a **value** ("what I hand over"). Query-key dot products, scaled and softmaxed, become weights, and the token takes that weighted blend of values. A causal mask stops tokens seeing the future. Because every token scores every earlier token, cost grows **quadratically** with context length, and past keys and values must be kept in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). Attention is also order-blind, so position has to be injected ([RoPE](#c/rope)). In DeepSeek-V3 each of 61 layers runs 128 heads, compressed with MLA. Nearly every efficiency trick in this map, from GQA and MLA to [DSA](#c/dsa) and FlashAttention, targets attention's memory and compute.
attention.article:
**Attention** is the mechanism that lets each token in a sequence pull in information from other tokens. In a [transformer](#c/transformer) it is the only component where positions interact. The [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) processes each token alone. Without attention, a model would see a bag of isolated words.

## How it works

At each [layer](#c/layer-stack), every token's current vector is projected three ways (see [query, key, value](#c/qkv)):

- **Query (Q):** what this token is looking for;
- **Key (K):** what each token advertises about itself;
- **Value (V):** the content a token hands over if selected.

For the current token, the model computes the dot product of its query with every earlier token's key, divides by the square root of the head dimension, and applies a softmax to get weights that sum to 1. The output is the weighted sum of those tokens' values. In matrix form, `softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V`. A **causal mask** blocks attention to later positions, which is what makes the model a next-token predictor.

The chat's analogy is a *soft database lookup*: instead of retrieving the one best match, you retrieve a blend weighted by how well each key matches.

## Many heads, every layer

One lookup can only capture one kind of relationship, so each layer runs many in parallel: [multi-head attention](#c/mha). DeepSeek-V3 uses 128 [heads](#c/heads) per layer across 61 layers, each with its own learned projections. Head outputs are concatenated and projected back into the [residual stream](#c/residual).

## Why it's expensive

Attention has two costs that grow with context:

| Cost | Scaling | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Score computation | O(L²) in sequence length L | Long prompts are slow to process |
| [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) memory | O(L) per request, per layer | Long contexts and big batches exhaust GPU memory |

During generation the second one dominates. Each new token must read every cached key and value from GPU memory, and the arithmetic per byte read is small. [Inference is therefore memory-bound](#c/memory-bound): the GPU waits on data, not math.

## Order-blindness

The attention formula doesn't care about token order: shuffle the keys and you get the same result. Position has to be supplied by [positional encoding](#c/position). Modern models use [RoPE](#c/rope), which rotates queries and keys so their dot product depends on relative distance. It can be stretched with [YaRN](#c/yarn) or omitted in some layers ([NoPE](#c/nope)).

## Ways people have reshaped it

- **Fewer K/V heads:** [MQA](#c/mqa) and [GQA](#c/gqa) share keys and values across query heads.
- **Compressed K/V:** [MLA](#c/mla) caches a 512-dim latent instead of full keys and values.
- **Sparse attention:** [DSA](#c/dsa) scores tokens with a cheap indexer and attends only to the top few, cutting O(L²) to O(L·k).
- **Linear/hybrid:** [linear attention](#c/linear-attn) or [state-space layers](#c/ssm) replace most full-attention layers.
- **Better kernels:** [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) computes the exact same result with far less memory traffic.

## From the chat

- Attention was described as "the only place tokens exchange information with each other," where context mixing happens.
- The chat framed the core serving problem as attention being memory-bound, not compute-bound. Most optimizations are "a scheme to move less data or move it less often."
- It split attention optimizations into *pure serving tricks* that work on frozen weights (FlashAttention, PagedAttention, KV quantization, prefix caching) and *architecture choices* baked in at training time (GQA/MQA, MLA, DSA).
- In MoE models attention stays dense: MoE replaces only the FFN, and every token still uses all the attention machinery.
- It noted the design space splits between GQA (Llama 4, Qwen3) and MLA (DeepSeek, Kimi K2), with sparse and linear attention as the emerging frontier.

heads.overview: An attention **head** is one complete query-key-value lookup, with its own learned projections turning each token's vector into *its* particular [Q, K and V](#c/qkv). One head can learn only one kind of relationship, so each layer runs many in parallel ([multi-head attention](#c/mha)). Their outputs are concatenated and projected back into the residual stream. DeepSeek-V3 has **128 heads in each of its 61 layers**, and every layer's heads are separate parameters. The key distinction is between **query heads** and **K/V heads**. Queries are used once and discarded, but keys and values are stored in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). So the number of K/V heads is the memory knob, and query heads are a compute and expressiveness knob. [MQA](#c/mqa) and [GQA](#c/gqa) exploit this by keeping many query heads while sharing few K/V heads.
heads.article:
An **attention head** is a single, self-contained instance of the attention lookup: a set of learned projection matrices that turn each token's vector into a query, a key and a value, followed by the score-softmax-blend computation. Transformers run many heads side by side in every [layer](#c/layer-stack), and the way heads are counted and shared is at the centre of most attention-efficiency work.

## What one head does

Given the token vectors entering a layer, a head applies three matrices to get, per token:

- a **query**, what this token is looking for ("I'm a verb, looking for my subject");
- a **key**, what the token advertises ("I'm a noun, I could be a subject");
- a **value**, what it hands over if matched.

The current token's query is compared with every earlier token's key, the scores are softmaxed into weights, and the head outputs a weighted blend of values. See [query, key, value](#c/qkv) for the details.

## Why many heads

A single head has one set of projections and so tends to learn one kind of relationship. Running many in parallel, [multi-head attention](#c/mha), lets different heads specialize. Illustratively, one might track subject-verb agreement, another pronoun reference, another nearby punctuation. Real heads are often messier and less interpretable than those tidy labels, but different heads do learn different patterns. The outputs of all heads are concatenated and mixed by an output projection.

Heads are **per layer**. Layer 3's heads and layer 20's heads are completely separate parameters, free to specialize at different levels of abstraction.

## DeepSeek-V3's heads

| Config field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `num_attention_heads` | 128 | Query heads per layer |
| `num_key_value_heads` | 128 | Nominally equal, since MLA does its compression elsewhere |
| `qk_nope_head_dim` | 128 | Content part of each query/key |
| `qk_rope_head_dim` | 64 | Separate positional slice ("decoupled RoPE") |
| `v_head_dim` | 128 | Width of each head's value |

Across 61 layers that is 7,808 heads in total.

## Query heads vs. K/V heads

When generating, the current token's query is used once and thrown away. Past tokens' **keys and values**, though, must be kept so future tokens can attend to them. That is the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). So:

- the number of **query heads** is a compute/expressiveness knob and costs nothing to cache;
- the number of **K/V heads** is the memory knob, because the cache stores one K and one V per K/V head, per token, per layer.

That asymmetry is what the attention variants exploit:

| Variant | Query heads | K/V heads | Cache vs. MHA |
|---|---|---|---|
| [MHA](#c/mha) | N | N | 1× |
| [GQA](#c/gqa) (e.g. 32 in 8 groups) | 32 | 8 | ¼ |
| [MQA](#c/mqa) | N | 1 | 1/N |
| [MLA](#c/mla) | 128 | (compressed latent) | ~1/32 in DeepSeek-V3 |

In a GQA model's config you see this directly: `num_key_value_heads` is much smaller than `num_attention_heads`. DeepSeek-V3 shows them equal because MLA's compression lives in other fields (`kv_lora_rank: 512`).

## From the chat

- The chat defined a head as "one complete instance of that whole query-key-value lookup," with its own learned projections.
- It explained "query heads" by the asymmetry: queries aren't cached, keys and values are, so K/V head count drives cache size.
- Worked example: 32 query heads in 8 groups of 4 means storing 8 K/V sets instead of 32, a 4× cache cut.
- Every layer has its own independent set of heads; "Layer 1's heads and Layer 7's heads share nothing."
- Exact head counts for closed models are undisclosed. The chat described the machinery but declined to give numbers for them.

kv-cache.overview: The **KV-cache** stores the key and value vectors of every past token, in every layer, so that each newly generated token can attend to them without recomputing them. Past keys and values never change, so caching them turns generation from quadratic recomputation into a lookup. The price is memory. The cache grows **linearly with context length and with batch size**, and for long contexts it can dwarf the model weights, making it the single biggest memory consumer in inference. Every decode step must also *read* the whole cache, which is a big reason [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Size scales with layers × K/V heads × head dim × tokens, which is why architectures shrink it at the source ([GQA](#c/gqa), [MLA](#c/mla), cross-layer sharing) and serving stacks manage it ([PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), [KV quantization](#c/kv-quant), [prefix caching](#c/prefix-cache)). The chat's summary: "nearly every inference optimization is ultimately a fight over the KV-cache."
kv-cache.article:
The **KV-cache** is the memory a transformer keeps during generation: the key and value vectors that every past token produced in every [attention](#c/attention) layer. It is what makes autoregressive generation practical, and it is the single largest consumer of GPU memory when serving an LLM.

## Why it exists

During [decoding](#c/decoding), the model produces one token at a time, and each new token attends to all previous tokens. The keys and values of those previous tokens don't change once computed, because causal attention means later tokens never affect earlier ones. So instead of recomputing them at every step, the model computes each token's K and V once and appends them to a cache. Each new step then only computes Q, K and V for the *new* token and reads the rest from memory.

Queries are *not* cached. The current token's query is used once and discarded. Only keys and values are needed again.

## How big it gets

For standard [multi-head attention](#c/mha), cache size per token is:

`2 (K and V) × layers × K/V heads × head_dim × bytes per number`

The total is then multiplied by tokens in context and by requests in the batch. It is **per layer**: every layer has its own heads and so its own cache. A 61-layer model caches 61 layers' worth.

Take a hypothetical MHA version of DeepSeek-V3's shape: 61 layers × 128 heads × 128 dims × 2 (K and V) is about 2 million numbers per token. At 16-bit precision that is roughly 4 MB per token, so a single 100K-token context would need hundreds of gigabytes. Hence the chat's point that for long contexts the cache "can dwarf the model weights themselves in memory."

## Why it's the bottleneck

Two things make the cache central to cost:

1. **Capacity.** GPU memory (HBM) not holding weights holds caches, so cache size caps how many requests can be batched together, and batch size drives tokens per GPU per second.
2. **Bandwidth.** Every decode step reads the entire cache for that request. There is little arithmetic per byte, so the GPU spends its time waiting on memory. That is the heart of [inference being memory-bound](#c/memory-bound).

## The lines of attack

| Approach | What it changes | Needs retraining? |
|---|---|---|
| [MQA](#c/mqa) / [GQA](#c/gqa) | Fewer K/V heads (many query heads share them) | Yes (architecture) |
| [MLA](#c/mla) | Cache a compressed latent (512 dims in DeepSeek-V3, ~32× smaller) | Yes |
| [Cross-layer KV sharing](#c/kv-sharing) | Adjacent layers share one cache | Yes |
| [DSA](#c/dsa) / sparse attention | Read only selected past tokens | Continued training |
| [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) | Store cache in pages, removing wasted reservations | No |
| [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) | 8-bit or lower instead of 16-bit | No |
| [Prefix caching](#c/prefix-cache) | Reuse a shared prefix's cache across requests | No |

The first group shrinks the cache at the source but has to be built in at training time. The second group are serving tricks that work on frozen weights, and they are part of how an already-deployed model gets cheaper over its life. [State-space models](#c/ssm) go further and replace the growing cache with a fixed-size state, at the cost of precise recall.

## From the chat

- The chat called the KV-cache "the central object" and "the single biggest memory consumer during inference," growing linearly with sequence length and batch size.
- "Nearly every inference optimization is ultimately a fight over the KV-cache."
- The cache exists per layer, because each layer's heads produce their own keys and values.
- It stressed that the number of *K/V* heads, not query heads, sets cache size, which is the whole trick behind MQA and GQA.
- DeepSeek-V3's config shows MLA caching a 512-dim latent versus 16,384 for naive full values across 128 heads, "the MLA memory win, in one number."

position.overview: **Positional encoding** exists because [attention](#c/attention) is order-blind: the score between two tokens depends only on their vectors, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical unless position is injected somehow. The original 2017 Transformer added fixed sinusoidal vectors to the embeddings, and early GPTs learned a position embedding per slot. Nearly every current model instead uses [RoPE](#c/rope), which *rotates* each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, so their dot product depends on relative distance. RoPE only works well over the positions seen in training, so extending context needs a rescaling: [Position Interpolation](#c/pi) or the frequency-aware [YaRN](#c/yarn). DeepSeek-V3 trained at 4,096 and stretched 40× to 163,840. Some models drop explicit encoding in some layers ([NoPE](#c/nope)) and let the causal mask carry order.
position.article:
**Positional encoding** is how a transformer learns the order of its input. It is needed because the core [attention](#c/attention) operation is permutation-invariant: it compares token vectors with dot products, and nothing in that arithmetic knows which token came first.

## Why attention needs help

Suppose you swap two tokens' vectors. Attention computes the same set of query-key scores, just in a different order, and produces the same blends. Without extra information, "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" are the same bag of vectors. The chat put it simply: attention "treats the input as a bag of tokens, so you have to inject position somehow."

The one exception is the **causal mask** in a decoder, which already reveals *something* about order: a token at position 100 can see 99 predecessors, one at position 5 only four. That observation is what makes [NoPE](#c/nope) possible.

## The main approaches

| Approach | Idea | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| Sinusoidal (absolute) | Add a fixed sine/cosine pattern per position to each embedding | Original 2017 Transformer |
| Learned absolute | Learn one vector per position slot, add it to the embedding | GPT-2/BERT generation |
| [RoPE](#c/rope) (rotary) | Rotate query and key pairs by a position-dependent angle; dot products then depend on relative distance | Nearly all current LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3 |
| [NoPE](#c/nope) | No explicit encoding; rely on the causal mask | Periodic layers in SmolLM3; full-attention blocks in Kimi Linear |

Absolute schemes tie a model to the positions it was trained on and give no direct notion of distance. RoPE's relative property, "these two tokens are 5 apart" regardless of where they sit, is a big part of why it won.

## The context-length problem

RoPE rotates coordinate pairs at a range of frequencies, set by a base (`rope_theta: 10000` in DeepSeek-V3). Fast-spinning pairs encode fine local distinctions, slow ones long-range position. A model trained on 4,096-token sequences has only ever seen the angles those positions produce. At position 8,000 the slow pairs reach angles never seen in training, and quality "falls off a cliff."

Training at long lengths from the start is very expensive, because attention cost grows with sequence length. So labs train short and **extend**:

- **[Position Interpolation](#c/pi):** divide every position by the extension factor so it lands back in the trained range. Simple, but it crowds the fast frequencies and blurs local precision.
- **[YaRN](#c/yarn):** frequency-aware interpolation. Leave fast pairs alone, squeeze slow ones, blend in between, and add an attention-temperature correction.

DeepSeek-V3 is a textbook case: `original_max_position_embeddings: 4096`, YaRN `factor: 40`, giving `max_position_embeddings: 163840`.

## Interactions with other techniques

- **[MLA](#c/mla):** RoPE doesn't survive MLA's low-rank compression cleanly, so DeepSeek splits each head into a 128-dim content part and a separate 64-dim positional part ("decoupled RoPE").
- **Hybrids and linear attention:** in models like Kimi Linear, the non-attention layers carry order implicitly, so the few full-attention layers can go without explicit encoding.

## Trade-offs and limits

Extended contexts are not free. A model stretched 40× generally uses the far end of its window less well than one genuinely trained at that length, so headline context lengths across models aren't directly comparable. Dropping position entirely (NoPE) is promising for length generalization but, per the chat, not yet standard in a major dense flagship.

## From the chat

- Attention is order-blind; position has to be injected.
- RoPE is "the method nearly every current model uses," and it rotates rather than adds.
- The chat walked through DeepSeek-V3's `rope_scaling` block: YaRN, factor 40, original 4,096, `beta_fast` 32, `beta_slow` 1, and `mscale` temperature fields.
- It warned that context extension "is not free lunch": effective use of the far end of a stretched window is often weaker than the headline number suggests.
- NoPE was flagged as a counterintuitive emerging idea, used in SmolLM3 (periodic layers) and Kimi Linear.

attn-kernel.overview: An **attention kernel** is the low-level GPU program that actually executes the [attention](#c/attention) math. It is the same formula, `softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V`, but it can be scheduled very differently on hardware. A naive kernel computes the full score matrix, writes it to the GPU's large but slow memory (HBM), reads it back for the softmax, writes again, and reads again to multiply by values. For long sequences that intermediate matrix is huge and the traffic dominates run time, because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Better kernels move less data. [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) tiles the computation into small blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM and fuses all the steps into one pass. [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) adapts the kernel to read a [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) scattered across pages. Kernel improvements change nothing about the model's weights or outputs. They are pure serving wins that apply to an already-trained model.

ffn.overview: The **feed-forward network (FFN)** is the second half of every transformer layer. It processes each token's vector **on its own**, with no cross-token interaction, by expanding it to a wider intermediate size, applying a nonlinearity, and projecting back down. It holds most of a dense model's parameters and is where much of the "stored knowledge" computation happens. In DeepSeek-V3 the first 3 layers use a dense FFN of width **18,432** (about 2.6× the 7,168 hidden size). The other 58 replace it with a **Mixture of Experts**: a [router](#c/router) picks 8 of 256 small [routed experts](#c/experts), each 7,168 → 2,048 → 7,168, plus one always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). MoE touches *only* the FFN; attention stays dense. That's how DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B parameters but runs only ~37B per token.
ffn.article:
The **feed-forward network (FFN)**, also called the MLP block, is the per-token computation inside each transformer [layer](#c/layer-stack). [Attention](#c/attention) moves information *between* tokens; the FFN then transforms each token's vector independently. In large models it is also where most parameters live, which is why [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) targets it.

## How it works

A classic FFN is two matrix multiplications with a nonlinearity between:

1. **Up-project** the token vector from the hidden size to a larger intermediate size;
2. apply a nonlinearity (modern models use gated variants such as SwiGLU, which add a third "gate" matrix);
3. **down-project** back to the hidden size, and add the result into the [residual stream](#c/residual).

Every token goes through the same weights, but separately: token 5's FFN computation never looks at token 6. The chat described the FFN as the place "a lot of the 'stored knowledge' computation happens." Facts and associations the model has memorized are largely encoded in these weights.

## Dense FFNs: DeepSeek-V3's first three layers

DeepSeek-V3's config sets `first_k_dense_replace: 3`, so layers 1–3 have ordinary dense FFNs with `intermediate_size: 18432`. That is about 2.6× the 7,168 hidden width, the normal expand-then-contract ratio. (Dense transformers commonly use around 4×; gated variants tend toward smaller ratios.)

## MoE FFNs: the other 58 layers

In the remaining 58 layers the single big FFN is replaced by many small ones:

| Part | Count | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| [Router](#c/router) | 1 per layer | Scores all 256 experts for each token |
| [Routed experts](#c/experts) | 256 per layer, 8 active per token | 7,168 → 2,048 → 7,168 each |
| [Shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) | 1 per layer, always active | Same slim shape |

A token arriving at a MoE layer is scored by the router, sent to its top 8 experts, and the weighted outputs plus the shared expert's are summed back into the residual stream.

Note the reversal: each expert's intermediate width (2,048) is *smaller* than the hidden size (7,168). That is deliberate **fine-grained** design ([fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained)): many small experts give the router finer-grained combinations than a few large ones. Llama 4 took the opposite approach, with fewer, larger experts (8,192 wide) and MoE only in alternate layers.

## Why the FFN is the one that gets split

- **It dominates parameters.** With a gated three-matrix FFN, one DeepSeek expert is about 3 × 7,168 × 2,048 ≈ 44M parameters. 256 of them across 58 layers is roughly 650B, most of the 671B total.
- **It is per-token.** Since the FFN never mixes tokens, different tokens can be sent to different weights with no coordination problem. Attention can't be split this way as easily, because every token must see the others.

The payoff is that DeepSeek-V3 activates only ~37B of its 671B parameters per token. Total parameters buy capacity; active parameters set the per-token cost. The trade-off is memory: all experts must sit in HBM even though most are idle for any given token.

## From the chat

- MoE "replaces *the FFN*, and only the FFN. Attention stays dense and shared."
- An "expert" is "just one of N parallel FFN weight-blocks," not a topic specialist.
- The chat explained what "expert intermediate dimension 2048" means: the temporary scratch width inside each expert, *smaller* than the 7,168 hidden size, unlike a dense FFN.
- From the real config: dense FFN `intermediate_size` 18,432 in the first 3 layers; `moe_intermediate_size` 2,048 for the experts in the other 58.
- The design split among open models is *granularity* (many small vs. few large experts) and whether to keep a shared expert.

router.overview: The **router** (or gate) is a tiny network in front of a Mixture-of-Experts [FFN](#c/ffn), essentially one learned linear layer. For each token's vector it produces a score for every expert, which amounts to a dot product with each expert's learned routing vector. It then keeps the **top-k** and sends the token only to those, weighting their outputs by the scores. It doesn't "know" anything semantic. The decision is made **fresh for every token at every MoE layer**, so in DeepSeek-V3 a single token gets 58 separate choices of 8 out of 256 [experts](#c/experts). Left alone, routing collapses onto a few favourite experts, so training adds an [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss). DeepSeek-V3 instead uses [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free), adjusting per-expert biases. Its config shows `scoring_func: "sigmoid"` and `topk_method: "noaux_tc"`.
router.article:
The **router**, also called the **gate**, decides which experts in a [Mixture-of-Experts](#c/moe) layer process each token. It is by far the smallest component of an MoE layer and the one that makes sparse activation possible.

## How it works

The router is essentially a single learned linear layer. For an incoming token vector (7,168 numbers in DeepSeek-V3) it computes one score per expert:

1. **Score.** Take the dot product of the token vector with each expert's learned routing vector, giving 256 numbers for DeepSeek-V3.
2. **Normalize.** Classic MoE applies a softmax; DeepSeek-V3 uses a sigmoid per expert (`scoring_func: "sigmoid"`).
3. **Select.** Keep the top-k experts. DeepSeek-V3 keeps 8 (`num_experts_per_tok: 8`); older designs kept 1 or 2, and [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) went to 1.
4. **Combine.** Send the token to those experts and sum their outputs weighted by the router scores, plus the always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) where one exists.

The chat stressed that there is no understanding involved: "The 'knowing' is just a dot product between the token's representation and each expert's learned routing vector."

## It re-decides every token, at every layer

Routing is independent per token and per MoE layer. In DeepSeek-V3, with 58 MoE layers, one token makes 58 separate routing decisions on its way up the stack, and the next token makes its own 58. "The" and "mitochondria" in the same sentence may land on entirely different experts at every layer. It is never "this prompt is about cooking, load the cooking experts." The active set churns constantly, which is why [experts](#c/experts) end up specializing in low-level token patterns rather than topics.

## The load-balancing problem

Unconstrained routing collapses into a feedback loop. Experts chosen slightly more often early in training get more gradient, get better, and get chosen even more. The result is a few overworked experts and many dead ones, which wastes most of the parameters. Fixes, roughly in historical order:

| Fix | How it works | Downside |
|---|---|---|
| [Auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss) | Extra training loss penalizing lopsided routing | Can degrade model quality |
| Expert capacity cap | Max tokens per expert per batch; overflow dropped or rerouted | Dropped tokens skip the FFN |
| [Auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) | Per-expert bias terms nudged up or down to even out load; they affect *selection* only | Extra bookkeeping |

DeepSeek-V3 uses the third. Its config's `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` literally means "no auxiliary loss." The biases shift which experts get picked, but the actual gating weights still come from pure token-expert affinity, so balancing doesn't distort the output mix.

## Systems cost

Routing also has an engineering cost. In large deployments experts are spread across many GPUs, so every MoE layer ships each token to wherever its chosen experts live and back again. That all-to-all communication, not the router's arithmetic, is the expensive part.

## Proprietary models

The mechanics above describe the published open architectures (Mixtral, DeepSeek and others). Closed frontier models are broadly understood to be MoE, but their routing schemes are not disclosed.

## From the chat

- The router was described as "essentially a single learned linear layer" producing a score per expert, then top-k.
- Routing "flips on every single token… and that's not a quirk, it's the whole design," at every layer independently.
- The chat corrected the "chemistry expert" picture: routing distributes computational sub-patterns, not topics.
- It explained load-balancing collapse ("two overworked experts and a roomful of dead ones") and the auxiliary-loss and capacity-cap fixes.
- In DeepSeek-V3's config, `scoring_func: "sigmoid"` and `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` are the auxiliary-loss-free balancing.

experts.overview: The **routed experts** are the many small feed-forward networks that replace a single big [FFN](#c/ffn) in each Mixture-of-Experts layer. DeepSeek-V3 has **256 per MoE layer** (58 such layers). For each token the [router](#c/router) activates **8**, and each chosen expert independently computes 7,168 → **2,048** → 7,168 with its own weights. Their router-weighted outputs, plus the always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c), are summed into the residual stream. Each expert is roughly 44M parameters, so the experts make up the bulk of DeepSeek-V3's 671B total while only ~37B are active per token. Experts are *not* topic specialists: inspection shows them specializing in low-level token patterns such as punctuation, number-like tokens or syntactic roles, re-chosen every token at every layer. DeepSeek goes for many small experts; [Llama 4](#c/llama4) for few large ones.
experts.article:
**Routed experts** are the parallel feed-forward sub-networks inside a [Mixture-of-Experts](#c/moe) layer. Only a few are used for any given token, which is how an MoE model can hold far more parameters than it computes with.

## How they work

In an MoE layer, the single dense [FFN](#c/ffn) is replaced by N smaller FFNs of identical shape, each with its own weights. For every token:

1. the [router](#c/router) scores all N experts;
2. the top-k are selected;
3. each selected expert runs the token vector through its own up-projection, nonlinearity and down-projection;
4. the outputs are weighted by the router scores and summed, along with any [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c), back into the [residual stream](#c/residual).

## DeepSeek-V3's experts

| Config field | Value |
|---|---|
| `n_routed_experts` | 256 |
| `num_experts_per_tok` | 8 |
| `n_shared_experts` | 1 |
| `moe_intermediate_size` | 2,048 |
| MoE layers | 58 of 61 |

So each token passes through 8 routed experts plus 1 shared at each of 58 layers, which is the "9 active experts" figure seen in articles. Each expert does 7,168 → 2,048 → 7,168. With a gated FFN of three matrices, that's about 44M parameters per expert, about 11B per layer's worth of routed experts, and about 650B across all MoE layers. Most of the 671B total lives in experts, and only ~37B is active per token.

## Small on purpose: fine-grained experts

A dense FFN usually expands to several times the hidden size; DeepSeek-V3's own dense layers use 18,432. The experts shrink to 2,048, *smaller* than the hidden size. This is **fine-grained** MoE ([fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained)). Splitting the same capacity into more, smaller experts and activating more of them gives the router far more possible combinations, so it can compose finer-grained behaviour. It is one of two main philosophies among open models:

| Model | Experts | Active | Expert width | MoE placement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) | 256 | 8 + 1 shared | 2,048 | All but first 3 layers |
| [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) | 128 | few, large | 8,192 | Alternating layers |
| [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) | 384 | (1T total, 32B active) | — | Keeps shared expert |
| [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) | 256 | 8 | — | 744B total / 40B active |

## What experts actually specialize in

The appealing mental model, "the router sends chemistry questions to the chemistry expert," is mostly wrong. When researchers inspect trained routers, the specialization is usually not human-interpretable topics. Experts tend to specialize in low-level, often syntactic or positional patterns: certain token types, punctuation, number-like tokens, structural roles. Since routing is redone every token at every layer, the active set churns constantly within a single sentence. Experts behave more like a distributed library of computational sub-patterns than a panel of specialists.

## Trade-offs

- **Memory, not compute.** All 256 experts per layer must sit in GPU memory even though 248 are idle for a given token.
- **Communication.** When experts are sharded across GPUs, tokens must be shipped to their experts and back at every layer.
- **Balance.** Without [load balancing](#c/lb-loss) or [loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free), a few experts hog the traffic and the rest go dead.

## From the chat

- The chat dismissed "experts are topic specialists" as "appealing and mostly false." They specialize in low-level token patterns and are re-chosen every token, every layer.
- The concrete picture: "a token hits a layer, the router picks 8 of 256 experts, each expert independently does 7168→2048→7168 with its own weights, and the 8 outputs (plus shared expert) are summed back into the residual stream."
- It explained why expert width (2,048) being smaller than hidden size (7,168) is "backwards from a normal FFN" and the whole point of fine-grained MoE.
- It framed the DeepSeek-vs-Llama 4 split as many small experts vs. few large ones, a genuinely different MoE philosophy.

shared-expert-c.overview: A **shared expert** is an [FFN](#c/ffn) expert that every token uses, bypassing the [router](#c/router), alongside the handful of routed [experts](#c/experts) it picks. The idea, popularized by DeepSeek, is that common general-purpose processing gets handled once by the shared expert, so the routed experts don't each have to redundantly relearn the basics and can specialize more sharply. DeepSeek-V3 has `n_shared_experts: 1`, the same slim 7,168 → 2,048 → 7,168 shape as its routed experts. That is why it is often described as having "9 active experts" (8 routed + 1 shared). Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 kept a shared expert; [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) dropped it, and the chat called whether it's needed "one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design right now." See [fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained) and [dropping the shared expert](#c/no-shared).

residual.overview: The **residual stream** is the running vector for each token that flows up the [layer stack](#c/layer-stack). Each sub-block, [attention](#c/attention) and then the [FFN](#c/ffn), reads a normalized copy of it and **adds** its output back, `x ← x + f(norm(x))`, rather than replacing it. Each layer therefore makes an *adjustment* to a shared workpiece. In DeepSeek-V3 the stream is 7,168 numbers wide (`hidden_size`) at every layer boundary, and the embedding writes into it first while the [output head](#c/output-head) reads it last. This design makes deep stacks trainable (gradients flow straight down the additive path), resists representation collapse, and explains why some layers can be near-identity. They add almost nothing, which is what makes [layer pruning](#c/layer-pruning) possible. It also enables the "logit lens": projecting the stream mid-way to peek at a premature guess.
residual.article:
The **residual stream** is the vector that represents each token as it passes through a transformer, together with the rule that every layer *adds to* it rather than overwriting it. It is less a component than an organizing principle, and it underlies the "refinement" view of how the [layer stack](#c/layer-stack) works.

## How it works

Each transformer block has two sub-blocks, each wrapped in a residual connection. In the pre-normalization form used by modern LLMs:

```
x = x + Attention(Norm(x))
x = x + FFN(Norm(x))
```

The sub-block sees a normalized copy of the stream and returns an *update*, which is added in. The chat's phrasing: "the input is added back to the output, so each layer makes an adjustment to the running representation rather than replacing it wholesale." Over 61 layers in DeepSeek-V3, the vector that began as the token's [embedding](#c/embedding) accumulates 122 such updates (one from [attention](#c/attention) and one from the [FFN](#c/ffn) per layer) before the [output head](#c/output-head) reads it.

## Its width

The stream's width is the model's `hidden_size`: 7,168 in DeepSeek-V3. Everything reads from and writes to vectors of that size. Internal sub-block widths can differ: the dense FFN expands to 18,432, each expert works in 2,048, and 128 heads × 128 value dims is 16,384. But each sub-block's output is projected back to 7,168 before being added. The chat called hidden size "*the* central dimension of the model."

## Why it matters

**Trainability.** The additive path gives gradients a direct route from the output back to early layers. That is a key reason very deep stacks train at all.

**Refinement, not replacement.** Because each layer only nudges the vector, the right mental model is an assembly line: "each station adds refinement to a single workpiece, and only the final station reads off the answer." Early layers tend to add local, surface-level information; later ones more abstract structure.

**Resisting collapse.** A known training concern is representation collapse, where successive layers stop differentiating. The chat noted that residual structure plus normalization are part of what prevents it, keeping layers making meaningful incremental edits.

**Near-identity layers.** The flip side: a layer whose update is tiny just passes the stream through almost unchanged. Research finds many middle and late layers in big models behave this way. That is why [layer pruning](#c/layer-pruning) can remove a meaningful fraction of layers with modest loss, and why [cross-layer sharing](#c/layer-sharing) and recurrent depth are even plausible.

## Peeking into the stream

Since the stream has the same shape at every layer, you can apply the output projection to an intermediate layer and see what the model "would" predict so far. This is the **logit lens**, or **early exit** when used for speed. It sometimes reveals a rough premature guess. The chat was clear this is a diagnostic or optimization trick. In normal operation only the final layer's stream becomes a prediction.

## In MoE layers

In a Mixture-of-Experts layer, the 8 routed [experts](#c/experts)' outputs, weighted by the [router](#c/router), and the [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c)'s output are all summed and added to the residual stream in one update, just like a dense FFN's output would be.

## From the chat

- "The thing flowing up the stack is often called the 'residual stream'" because each layer nudges a shared representation rather than starting over.
- Hidden size 7,168 was defined as "the width of the residual stream."
- The residual structure explains near-redundant layers: "a layer that adds almost nothing just passes the representation through largely unchanged."
- Residuals and normalization were credited with preventing representation collapse.
- The logit lens was the one nuance to "only the last layer predicts": a way to peek, not how the model works.

output-head.overview: The **output head** (unembedding, or LM head) is the final projection that turns the top of the [residual stream](#c/residual) into a prediction. It multiplies the last layer's 7,168-wide vector for the current position by a 7,168 × 129,280 matrix in DeepSeek-V3, producing one score (**logit**) per vocabulary [token](#c/tokenizer). A softmax turns those into probabilities, and the [decoding loop](#c/decoding) samples the next token, often shaped by temperature or top-p. This is the **only** place a prediction happens. The 61 layers below never each guess and blend; they refine one vector. Some models tie this matrix to the input [embedding](#c/embedding); DeepSeek-V3's weights list them separately. [Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp) adds extra prediction modules that forecast further ahead during training and can draft tokens at inference.
output-head.article:
The **output head**, also called the **unembedding** or **LM head**, is the last step of a transformer's forward pass. It converts the model's internal representation into a score for every token in the vocabulary. Everything before it builds a representation; this is where a prediction is actually made.

## How it works

After the final [layer](#c/layer-stack), the model takes the [residual stream](#c/residual) vector at the last position, applies a final normalization, and multiplies it by a matrix of shape `hidden_size × vocab_size`:

- DeepSeek-V3: 7,168 × 129,280, about 0.93B parameters;
- output: 129,280 **logits**, one per [token](#c/tokenizer) in the vocabulary;
- a **softmax** converts logits into a probability distribution that sums to 1.

The [decoding loop](#c/decoding) then picks the next token. It might take the argmax (greedy), or sample with a **temperature** that sharpens or flattens the distribution, sometimes restricted to the most likely candidates (top-k / top-p). The chosen token is appended and the whole forward pass runs again.

## Only one prediction

This is the component that clears up a common misconception. The layers do **not** each predict a token that then gets blended. The chat's correction: "there's exactly **one** prediction, made at the top, from the final layer's output. The intermediate layers never produce token predictions in normal operation; they produce *representations*."

You *can* apply the output head to an intermediate layer's vector (the "logit lens" or "early exit") and sometimes read off a rough, premature guess. That's useful for interpretability and for some speed tricks, but it isn't how standard inference works.

## Tied or untied

The output head has the same shape as the input [embedding](#c/embedding) table, transposed. Some models **tie** them, using one matrix for both directions, which saves parameters and matters most in small models where these matrices are a big share of the total. DeepSeek-V3's published weights list the input and output embeddings separately from the 61 hidden layers.

## Training signal

During [pre-training](#c/pretraining), the output head's probabilities at *every* position are compared with the actual next token, and the cross-entropy loss is backpropagated through the whole stack. That one-step-ahead objective is the whole training signal of a plain language model.

## Extensions

**[Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp).** DeepSeek-V3 adds a small sequential prediction module (`num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`) that, during training, also predicts the token after next. It keeps a causal chain, so the second prediction builds on the first. That gives a denser training signal, and at inference the extra module can propose a draft token for [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding).

**[Large Concept Model](#c/lcm).** A more radical research direction predicts whole sentence-level "concept" embeddings instead of individual tokens.

**[Diffusion LMs](#c/diffusion-lm).** These drop the one-token-at-a-time head altogether and refine a whole block of tokens in parallel.

## Cost notes

For a large model the output head is a small share of total compute, but it scales with vocabulary size. It is one reason vocabulary size is a real design trade-off: a bigger vocabulary means shorter sequences but a bigger final matrix and softmax at every step.

## From the chat

- "Only after the final layer do you take the resulting vector, run it through one last projection (the 'unembedding,' into vocabulary-sized logits), and turn it into a probability distribution over the next token."
- The chat corrected the belief that "each layer predicts the next token and those get blended." Its analogy was "less like '12 voters each guessing'… more like an assembly line."
- It raised the logit lens / early exit as the honest nuance.
- DeepSeek-V3's MTP (`num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`) was described as a training objective whose extra heads "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference."

serving.overview: The **serving system** is the software and hardware stack that runs a trained model for many users at once, and it is where much of a frozen model's cost reduction happens. It loads the weights onto accelerators (for DeepSeek-V3, all 671B parameters must sit in HBM even though only ~37B are active per token), [batches](#c/batching) requests together, runs the prefill and [decoding loop](#c/decoding), and manages the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). A modern stack, in the chat's summary, runs a GQA or MLA model with [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) kernels, under [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) memory management, with prefix caching, often KV quantization, low-precision weights (FP8/INT8/INT4) and continuous batching. None of these change the weights, so they make an already-deployed model cheaper over its life. Open stacks like vLLM are well documented, but providers like Anthropic and OpenAI don't publish theirs.

batching.overview: **Batching** means running many requests through the model at the same time so the accelerator stays busy. During generation each step must stream the model's weights from GPU memory, and for a single request that is a lot of data movement for very little arithmetic, because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Processing a batch of requests together reuses each weight read across all of them, so throughput (tokens per GPU per second) rises steeply and cost per token falls. The limit is memory: every request in the batch needs its own [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), which is why cache-shrinking tricks ([GQA](#c/gqa), [MLA](#c/mla), [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), KV quantization) translate directly into bigger batches and cheaper tokens. [Continuous batching](#c/cont-batching) goes further, swapping finished requests out and new ones in at every step instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish. The chat listed "better batching" first among the ways a frozen model gets cheaper to serve.

weights-precision.overview: **Numeric precision** is how many bits each stored number uses. Models are commonly trained and served in 16-bit formats (BF16/FP16), but weights, activations and the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) can be stored in **FP8, INT8 or INT4**, halving or quartering memory. Since decoding is limited by how fast bytes move out of GPU memory ([inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound)), fewer bytes per parameter means faster tokens as well as more room for batching. The chat listed quantization, "running the model at lower numerical precision, FP8/INT8/INT4, often with negligible quality loss", as a major way a frozen model gets cheaper to serve. DeepSeek-V3 went further: FP8 is native to its training framework, so its config reads `quant_method: "fp8"` and it ships FP8 weights, with a conversion script if you want BF16. Post-hoc compression is covered under [weight quantization](#c/quantization) and [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant).

decoding.overview: The **decoding loop** is how a transformer generates text: **one token at a time**. After a **prefill** pass processes the whole prompt in parallel and fills the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), each decode step runs the full stack for just the newest token, reads every cached key and value, gets next-token probabilities from the [output head](#c/output-head), samples one token, appends it, and repeats. Each step depends on the previous one, so steps can't be parallelized within a request, and each must stream the active weights and the whole cache from memory for very little arithmetic. That is why decode is [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), and why long reasoning chains are costly: every thinking token is sequential. [Speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding) has a cheap drafter propose several tokens for the big model to verify at once, and DeepSeek's MTP module can serve as that drafter. [Diffusion LMs](#c/diffusion-lm) abandon strict left-to-right generation altogether.

qkv.overview: **Query, key and value** are the three vectors every token produces in each attention head, via three learned projection matrices. The chat's soft-database analogy: the **query** is what the current token is looking for ("I'm a verb, looking for my subject"), each token's **key** advertises what it offers ("I'm a noun, I could be a subject"), and the **value** is the content it hands over if matched. The query is dotted with every earlier key, the scores are scaled and softmaxed into weights, and the output is the weighted blend of values. Crucially, a query is used once and discarded, while keys and values of past tokens are needed by every future token, so only K and V go into the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). That asymmetry is why [GQA](#c/gqa) and [MQA](#c/mqa) cut K/V heads but keep query heads. In DeepSeek-V3 each query/key has 128 content dims plus a 64-dim [RoPE](#c/rope) slice.
qkv.article:
**Query (Q), key (K) and value (V)** are the three roles each token plays inside an [attention head](#c/heads). Every token's vector is multiplied by three separately learned matrices to produce one vector for each role, and the interplay between them is what lets a token gather information from the rest of the sequence.

## The soft database lookup

The chat's analogy is a database lookup where you get a *blend* of results instead of one exact match:

| Vector | Role | Illustration |
|---|---|---|
| **Query** | What the current token is looking for | "I'm a verb, I'm looking for my subject" |
| **Key** | What each token advertises | "I'm a noun, I could be a subject" |
| **Value** | What a token hands over if matched | the actual content it contributes |

In short: *query = what I'm looking for, key = what I advertise, value = what I hand over.*

## How the computation runs

For one head and the current token *t*:

1. Compute `q_t`, and for every earlier token *i*, `k_i` and `v_i`.
2. Score each earlier token: `s_i = q_t · k_i / √d`, where *d* is the head dimension. The scaling keeps scores from growing with dimension.
3. Softmax the scores into weights that sum to 1. A causal mask gives future tokens zero weight.
4. Output `Σ weight_i · v_i`, a blend of values dominated by the best-matching keys.

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back to the [residual stream](#c/residual) width.

### A tiny example

Suppose three earlier tokens have scores 2.0, 0.5 and −1.0 against the current query. Softmax gives weights of roughly 0.79, 0.18 and 0.04, so the output is mostly the first token's value with a little of the second's. Nothing is a hard yes/no; every earlier token contributes in proportion to its match.

## Why only K and V get cached

During [decoding](#c/decoding), the query of the current token is used once, for this step, and is never needed again. But the keys and values of every past token are needed by *every future token*. So:

- **K and V are cached** in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), per token, per head, per layer;
- **Q is not.**

This asymmetry drives an entire family of designs:

- [Multi-head attention](#c/mha): one K/V pair per query head, the full cache.
- [Multi-Query Attention](#c/mqa): all query heads share one K/V head, so the cache is about N× smaller.
- [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa): query heads in groups share K/V. With 32 query heads in 8 groups, the cache is 4× smaller.
- [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla): cache a compressed latent from which K and V are reconstructed.

## Position lives in Q and K

Attention on its own ignores order. [RoPE](#c/rope) fixes this by rotating the query and key vectors by position-dependent angles before the dot product, so the score depends on how far apart two tokens are. Values are not rotated. In DeepSeek-V3 each query and key has a 128-dim content part (`qk_nope_head_dim`) plus a separate 64-dim positional part (`qk_rope_head_dim`), while values are 128-dim (`v_head_dim`). That split exists because MLA's compression would otherwise scramble the rotation.

## From the chat

- The chat introduced Q/K/V with the soft-database analogy and the verb/subject example.
- It defined a head as "one complete instance of that whole query-key-value lookup," with its own learned projections.
- It made the key point that "the thing you cache is the keys and values, not the queries," which is why K/V head count, not query head count, sets cache size.
- It noted that head specializations like "subject-verb agreement" are illustrative; real heads are often messier.

mha.overview: **Multi-head attention (MHA)** is the standard attention design from the 2017 Transformer: each layer runs many independent [heads](#c/heads) in parallel, each with its own query, key and value projections, so each can learn a different relationship (loosely, one tracking subject-verb links, another pronoun reference). Outputs are concatenated and projected back into the residual stream. The original Transformer used 8 heads; DeepSeek-V3 has 128 per layer across 61 layers. In plain MHA every query head has its own K/V head, so the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) stores K and V for all of them. That is the most expressive option and the most memory-hungry. The later variants all reduce that cost: [MQA](#c/mqa) shares one K/V head, [GQA](#c/gqa) shares one per group, and [MLA](#c/mla) compresses K/V into a latent.
mha.article:
**Multi-head attention (MHA)** runs several attention lookups ("heads") side by side in each [layer](#c/layer-stack), each with its own learned projections, and combines their results. It was introduced with the original Transformer in 2017 and remains the conceptual baseline that every later attention variant is measured against.

## How it works

Given the token vectors entering a layer (width *d*), MHA:

1. projects each token into a query, key and value **for every head**, each head using its own three matrices;
2. runs scaled dot-product [attention](#c/attention) separately in each head;
3. concatenates the heads' outputs;
4. applies an output projection to mix them and return a vector of width *d* to the [residual stream](#c/residual).

Heads are typically narrow (head dim is often 64 or 128), so many of them together cost about the same as one wide head. What you gain is several *independent* views of the sequence.

## Why multiple heads

One head has one set of Q/K/V projections, so it tends to learn one kind of relationship. With many heads, each can specialize. The chat's illustrative examples: one head tracking subject-verb agreement, another following which pronoun refers to which noun, another attending to nearby punctuation. Those clean labels are illustrative; real heads are messier and often not neatly interpretable. The principle that different heads learn different relationships holds, though.

Every layer has its **own** fresh set of heads. Layer 3's might do low-level syntactic linking while layer 20's track discourse-level relationships.

## Scale over time

| Model | Heads per layer | Layers |
|---|---|---|
| Original Transformer (2017, base) | 8 | 6 encoder + 6 decoder |
| DeepSeek-V3 | 128 | 61 |

Closed frontier models don't publish head counts.

## The cost: one K/V pair per query head

In plain MHA, query heads and K/V heads come in matched sets: N query heads, N key heads, N value heads. During generation, past keys and values are stored in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), so the cache holds K and V for all N heads, in every layer, for every token. For long contexts and large batches, that cache becomes the dominant memory cost and the main drag on [serving](#c/serving) throughput.

## What came after

MHA's cache cost motivated a sequence of variants:

| Variant | Idea | Cache vs. MHA |
|---|---|---|
| [MQA](#c/mqa) (2019) | All query heads share a single K/V head | ~1/N; quality can dent |
| [GQA](#c/gqa) (2023) | Query heads in groups, one K/V head per group | e.g. ¼ with 32 heads in 8 groups |
| [MLA](#c/mla) (2024) | Cache a compressed latent, reconstruct per-head K/V | ~1/32 in DeepSeek-V3 |
| [DSA](#c/dsa) (2025) | Attend only to top-selected past tokens (on top of MLA) | Less read per step |

All of these keep MHA's many *query* heads, because queries aren't cached, and cut or compress the *key/value* side.

A curiosity: DeepSeek-V3's config lists `num_attention_heads: 128` and `num_key_value_heads: 128`, which looks like plain MHA. It isn't. MLA's compression is expressed through other fields (`kv_lora_rank: 512`). A GQA model like Llama 4 shows `num_key_value_heads` well below `num_attention_heads`.

## From the chat

- The chat explained "multi-head attention" as running multiple Q/K/V heads in parallel in every layer, "each learns to attend to a different pattern," concatenated so the layer gets "many 'views' of the token relationships at once."
- It noted that in standard MHA "there are as many query heads as there are key/value heads," and that is the inefficiency MQA and GQA exploit.
- It warned that tidy head roles are illustrative, not literal.
- It flagged that DeepSeek-V3's equal head counts don't mean plain MHA, because MLA works through separate config fields.

mqa.overview: **Multi-Query Attention (MQA)**, proposed by Noam Shazeer in 2019, keeps all N query heads of [multi-head attention](#c/mha) but collapses keys and values to a **single shared K/V head**. Every query still asks its own question, but they all look up against the same keys and values. Since only K and V are stored in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), the cache shrinks by roughly **N×**: with 32 heads, 1/32 of the memory. That means far more concurrent requests or longer contexts per GPU, and less data read per decode step. The catch is expressiveness. Forcing every query to share one K/V view can dent quality, and training can be less stable.
